title: Solar Power Design and Installation Basics
desc: Learn to size, design and plan a small solar system with correct safety, cost, layout and handover.
outcomes: Explain how panels, inverters and batteries work together.
Size a small system from a load list.
Produce a design pack and handover sheet.
task: Design a small rooftop solar system for a practice home or shop, with load list, size, layout, safety plan, cost, payback and handover sheet.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, a floor plan or satellite view, two peers and a licensed electrician mentor. Installation on live wiring is done only by licensed people.
standard: Load list and size are correct; roof and shade checks are done; protective devices and earthing are listed; cost and payback shown; a licensed person signs the design; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Trainee electricians, technicians, small shop owners, community energy workers.
evidence: load list, sizing sheet, layout drawing, safety plan, cost sheet, handover sheet
modules: How a solar system works
Understand
Panels make direct current, an inverter changes it to usable power, and protection keeps people and wiring safe.
Panels produce power from light; output falls with shade, heat and dust.
Grid-tied systems feed the building and the grid; off-grid systems need batteries.
The inverter matches voltage and frequency and shuts down if the grid fails.
Meters, breakers and earthing complete the system.
A 3 kW array in a sunny place makes about 4 kWh per kW per day, so around 12 kWh a day.
Draw a block diagram of a grid-tied system.
Diagram shows panels, isolator, inverter, protection, meter and load in order.
Load list
Apply
List every device before you size anything.
Record watts and hours used each day for each device.
Add starting surge for motors.
Separate essential loads from others.
Total energy per day = sum of watts x hours.
A shop has 6 lights at 10 W for 10 hours (0.6 kWh), 2 fans at 60 W for 8 hours (0.96 kWh) and a fridge using 1.5 kWh a day. Total is 3.06 kWh a day.
Make a load list for a practice shop.
Every device is listed with watts and hours and the total is correct.
Site survey
Analyse
The roof and the wiring decide what is possible.
Measure usable roof area, tilt and direction.
Check shade at morning, noon and afternoon.
Inspect roof strength and old wiring.
Photograph and record the main panel.
A roof with 16 usable square metres facing south fits about eight panels of 2 square metres; a water tank shades two panels in the afternoon and they are moved.
Complete a survey sheet for a practice roof.
Area, tilt, shade and panel condition are recorded with photos or sketches.
Sizing the system
Apply
Match energy need, sunshine and losses to a panel count.
Array kW = daily kWh / (sun hours x 0.75 efficiency).
Choose an inverter close to array size.
Check voltage and current limits of the inverter.
Check the roof can carry the number of panels.

A shop using 3.06 kWh a day with 5 sun hours needs 3.06 / (5 x 0.75) = 0.82 kW, so two panels of 450 W (0.9 kW) cover it on paper. The owner adds margin for dust and ageing and chooses three panels, 1.35 kW.
Size the array and inverter for your load list.
Formula, numbers and margin are shown and limits are checked.
Electrical protection and earthing
Apply
Protection prevents fire and shock.
Direct current isolator, alternating current breaker and surge protection.
Correct cable size and colour for the current and distance.
Earth the frames and the system to the correct standard.
Label every switch and cable.
A cable too thin for the current heats up; the design uses the next size up and keeps the voltage drop within the allowed limit.
Draw a single line diagram with protection.
All protective devices are present and sized, and earthing is shown.
Safety on site
Evaluate
Work at height and live electricity can kill.
Use harness, edge protection and safe ladders.
Isolate and lock out before any work; test for dead.
Never work alone on the roof; watch for heat and rain.
Only licensed people connect to the main supply.
A team stops work when wind rises because a panel acts like a sail and can pull a worker off the roof.
Write a site safety plan for one install day.
Plan covers height, electrical, weather, roles and emergency steps.
Cost and payback
Evaluate
Show the owner what it costs and when it pays back.
List panels, inverter, mounting, cables, protection and labour.
Annual saving = kWh made x price per kWh.
Payback = cost / annual saving.
Include maintenance and inverter replacement.
A 1.35 kW system costing 90,000 saves about 1,800 kWh a year at 8 per kWh, 14,400 a year. Payback is about 6.3 years.
Build the cost and payback table.
Costs add up, assumptions are listed and payback is correct.
Design pack and handover
Create
Hand over clear documents so the owner can use and maintain the system.
Include load list, layout, single line diagram and cost.
Give a user guide and a cleaning and check schedule.
Record serial numbers and warranties.
Explain what to do if the system trips.
The owner receives a folder and a one-page card by the inverter listing who to call and what lights mean.
Assemble the full design pack.
All documents are present, consistent and understandable to a non-technical owner.
quiz: What converts DC to AC?
Inverter. (Covered in module 1: How a solar system works. To pass that module: Diagram shows panels, isolator, inverter, protection, meter and load in order.)
kWh equals?
kW times hours. (Covered in module 2: Load list. To pass that module: Every device is listed with watts and hours and the total is correct.)
Name a shading effect.
Output drops. (Covered in module 1: How a solar system works. To pass that module: Diagram shows panels, isolator, inverter, protection, meter and load in order.)
Panel sizing formula?
Daily kWh / (sun hours x efficiency). (Covered in module 4: Sizing the system. To pass that module: Formula, numbers and margin are shown and limits are checked.)
Name two protective devices.
Breaker and surge protector. (Covered in module 5: Electrical protection and earthing. To pass that module: All protective devices are present and sized, and earthing is shown.)
Who may wire live circuits?
Licensed electricians. (Covered in module 6: Safety on site. To pass that module: Plan covers height, electrical, weather, roles and emergency steps.)
Why label everything?
Safe maintenance and emergency. (Covered in module 5: Electrical protection and earthing. To pass that module: All protective devices are present and sized, and earthing is shown.)
Payback formula?
Cost / yearly saving. (Covered in module 7: Cost and payback. To pass that module: Costs add up, assumptions are listed and payback is correct.)
Why cut waste first?
Smaller, cheaper system. (Covered in module 2: Load list. To pass that module: Every device is listed with watts and hours and the total is correct.)
Are panels live in daylight?
Yes. (Covered in module 6: Safety on site. To pass that module: Plan covers height, electrical, weather, roles and emergency steps.)
rubric: Load list, kWh per day and panel count shown step by step
Working checked by a second person, with margin and losses explained
Wiring code, permit and inspector steps for the place are written down
Code rules cited and a licensed installer has signed off the design
